reference.source: ILAE classification / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in KCNQ2 encoding the Kv7.2 voltage-gated potassium channel subunit that carries the neuronal M-current
The encephalopathy form usually presents in the first days of life with frequent tonic seizures, often with focal or asymmetric features
The interictal EEG is typically markedly abnormal, and a burst-suppression or multifocal pattern may be seen
It sits at the severe end of a spectrum whose benign end is self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy, also caused by KCNQ2 variants
Sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure medications are often particularly effective in this potassium channelopathy, unlike in sodium-channel loss-of-function disorders
Brain MRI may show reversible signal changes in the basal ganglia and thalamus in the neonatal period
Development is impaired, though outcome varies with the specific variant and its functional effect
reference.pathophysiology: KCNQ2 encephalopathy is caused by pathogenic variants, frequently dominant-negative or gain- and loss-of-function missense changes, in KCNQ2 encoding the Kv7.2 potassium channel subunit. Kv7.2 combines with Kv7.3 to generate the M-current, a slow potassium current that stabilises the resting membrane potential and limits repetitive firing. Disruption of this current increases neuronal excitability in the neonatal brain, producing early tonic seizures and a severe epileptic encephalopathy, in contrast to the milder self-limited phenotype seen with less disruptive variants.
additionalDifferentials: Inborn errors of metabolism presenting in the neonate
Structural neonatal seizures from malformation or stroke
additionalInvestigations: KCNQ2 testing or a neonatal epilepsy gene panel or exome sequencing
EEG documenting the interictal pattern and seizure semiology
Brain MRI, which may show transient basal ganglia and thalamic signal change
Metabolic screening to exclude treatable causes of neonatal seizures
Developmental follow-up to track the encephalopathic course
redFlags: Frequent neonatal tonic seizures with a severely abnormal interictal EEG
Refractoriness to standard first-line neonatal seizure treatment
Evidence of developmental arrest in early infancy
Diagnostic uncertainty between the benign and encephalopathic ends of the spectrum
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies with the underlying variant: many children with the encephalopathy form have intellectual disability and persistent epilepsy, though seizures may improve over the first years. Early recognition and use of sodium-channel-blocking therapy can improve seizure control in responsive cases.
pitfalls: Assuming all KCNQ2 neonatal seizures are benign and self-limited
Avoiding sodium-channel blockers, which are often the most effective agents here
Misreading transient neonatal MRI signal change as an alternative diagnosis
Delaying genetic testing in an unexplained neonatal epileptic encephalopathy
